summary: The Oregon Environmental Council generally commends the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation's impact statement on ORV use, praising its fairness and the restrictions placed on National Parks. However, they raise two main objections: the statement lacks enforceable noise standards (recommending a maximum of 73 decibels at 50 feet), and they oppose the 'monitor after the fact' approach to determining ORV compatibility with land resources, insisting that studies be conducted before ORV use is permitted in any area.

statement.text:
Dear Mr. Hofe:
We wish to commend the Bureau of Outdoor Recreation for its fair and well-developed impact statement dealing with the Off Road Vehicles (ORV) problem. With a few exceptions the statement reflects the concerns we as conservationists share toward the use of the ORV.
We are particularly pleased with the policy established for ORV use in the National Parks. We are impressed by the restrictions and would encourage the BOR to place this type of control on all lands. However, we realize the ORV is here to stay and no matter how strongly we object, the ORV users have a right to use the public lands. They have a right to use them, but not destroy them. We hope the Department of the Interior controls can prevent any destruction.
There are two areas, however, that we must object to and encourage revisions in the policy. The first is the treatment of noise. The statement recognizes that there is a real problem, but makes no effort to minimize the levels. The most stringent statement concerning noise is found on page 5. "An ORV that produces unusual or excessive noise shall not be permitted on Interior lands." The problem here is that there is no indication as to what is considered excessive so enforcement would be extremely difficult.
The problem of noisy ORVs, particularly snowmobiles, is regarded as one of the greatest problems with the vehicles. The Washington State Parks and Recreation Commission says, in its publication "Snowmobiling in Washington State" that "Probably the greatest concern relating to snowmobiles is noise encroachment in a naturally quiet environment." Here is where ORV users encroach upon the rights of other recreation users. How noisy are these machines? The level of the snowmobile is about 112 decibels at the operator's ear. That is over standards set up under Walsh-Healy

Letter to Mr. G. Douglas Hofe, Jr. July 6, 1972 Page 2
18
for a 30-minute per day period. At 50 feet the noise level is about 86 decibels, which is just below the maximum for an eight hour period. Not too many non-users will suffer hearing loss from these machines but the noise levels at which they operate certainly indicates they could do a rather thorough job of destroying the peace and quiet of an outdoor area.
Why are these machines not quieter? A Conservation Foundation publication by Malcolm F. Baldwin entitled "The Off-Road Vehicle and Environmental Quality" attributes the reason to what the American buyer wants. Industry representatives say they could be made half as noisy but they would not sell. The Oregon Environmental Council recommends that BOR establish stringent noise restrictions in order to force the ORV industry into using a quieter machine. We suggest a maximum level of 73 decibels at 50 feet. This will not alleviate the problem by any means but it will help control it and possibly cut down the antagonism between ORV users and other more traditional recreation users.
Our second main objection to the statement is found on pp. 12-13. Reference is made to the negative environmental impact on the areas. Mention is made of the difficulty of determining the levels of use compatible with the resource. The method of determination is to monitor effects of ORV use on the lands to discover this data. We find this unacceptable. Extensive studies should be made of the areas before ORV use is allowed. If the monitor method is implemented, once it is found that the ORV is non-compatible with the resource, it will be too late. This determination must be made before ORV use is allowed.
Page 7 of the report discusses public review of the area policies before implementation. This would be a good time to conduct these studies to determine if use is compatible with the area. We commend the BOR for allowing public review and we encourage them to follow through with this proposal.
The Oregon Environmental Council is very concerned with the ORV problem and the potential damage they can cause to the environment. Generally we approve of the impact statement but encourage that there be:
. More stringent noise restrictions on the vehicles; and
. Better review before allowing the vehicles into an area.
Sincerely,
(Larry Williams
Executive Director
